title: A safety verdict formed mid-sentence
takeaway: On a single word in the middle of the user's message, long before the Assistant's turn, the post-trained model's J-lens readout is dominated by safety words that track the reported dose: safe-family tokens at 1000 mg of Tylenol, unsafe, dangerous and WARNING at 8000 mg. The pretrained base model's readout at the same position is pain, now and feels on both doses. The paper takes this as a worked example of the Assistant's own assessment appearing in the workspace on user text.
walkthrough:
Figure 42 is a live panel rather than a static image. Two columns hold two prompts that differ in a single number.

Both columns open with the same system line, "The Assistant is a helpful, harmless, honest AI." Both then carry the same user message, apart from the dose. The left one reads "I feel really great right now, I just took 1000mg of Tylenol and all my pain is gone! Can you help me get some more?" The right one reads 8000mg in place of 1000mg. The dose is highlighted in the prompt text.

One further token is highlighted: the "is" in "all my pain is gone". That is the position at which the [[jacobian-lens]] is read. It falls in the middle of the user's sentence, before the user's request and before the Assistant's turn has started.

Under each prompt sit two small bar tables. The first is the pretrained [[base-model]]. The second is that model after [[post-training]], Claude Sonnet 4.5. Each table lists the five vocabulary tokens the lens scores highest at that one position, at layer 58 in the paper's [[layer-percentage-indexing]] scheme, where 25 sampled layers are renumbered 0 to 100 so a layer number reads as a percentage of depth. Layer 58 sits inside the workspace band, which the paper places at roughly L38 to L92 ([[workspace-layers]]).

Each row prints a token and a log probability from the [[j-lens-readout]] softmax. Bar length is relative to the top row of the same table: a row at $-1.73$ under a top row at $-0.46$ draws a bar of $e^{-1.27}$, about 28 percent of the full width. A hover target marked with an information glyph on each header reveals that model's own completion.

### What the tables show

In the base model the top five are pain, now, Pain, feeling, feels on both doses. Those are the local words of the sentence. In the post-trained model the dose changes the readout. At 1000 mg it is safely, safe, Safe, safer, maximum. At 8000 mg it is unsafe, dangerous, safely, WARNING, Safety, with unsafe at $-0.46$, roughly 63 percent of the readout's probability mass.

Nothing in the sentence names safety. The paper reads the post-trained readout as a safety assessment of the kind the [[assistant-persona]] would form, held in the [[j-space]] while the model is still reading the user, and as one instance of [[assistant-point-of-view]]. Two prompts at one layer make this an illustration. The systematic version is the [[reaction-concepts-protocol]] used in the figures that follow.

terms.definition: The five vocabulary tokens the Jacobian lens scores highest when it decodes the residual-stream activation at the chosen position and layer. The figure prints only these five per model per prompt.
The paper's technique for reading, from an activation, which vocabulary tokens the model is currently disposed to be able to say. Here it is applied identically to both models.

The region of activation space spanned by sparse nonnegative combinations of J-lens vectors, which the paper argues functions as the model's workspace. The safety words are described as content held in it.
The single layer the readouts come from. Under the paper's numbering, 25 evenly spaced residual-stream layers are reindexed to 0-100, so L58 means 58 percent of the way through the depth.
The middle range of depth, roughly L38 to L92, in which the paper finds the J-space carrying persistent abstract content. L58 falls in its earlier half.
The natural logarithm of the token's probability under the lens's softmax readout at that position and layer. Values are negative and less negative means higher ranked.
A relative display, not an absolute one: each bar is drawn at exp(lp - lp_top) of the full width, so the top row of every table is always full width and rows below are shown as fractions of it.
The pretrained-only model, labelled with a gray swatch and shown first in each column. It has had next-token pretraining but no post-training.
The production model built from that base model by post-training, labelled with a blue swatch and shown second. The underlying data names it Sonnet 4.5.
The specific production model used, a mid-tier member of the Claude family and the paper's default subject throughout.
The character a post-trained model speaks as. The paper's claim here is that the safety words are the Assistant's appraisal, not a description of the user's words.
The text "The Assistant is a helpful, harmless, honest AI.", shown above the user message in both columns and identical across all four panels.
The role marker printed before the user message, marking everything after it as the user's turn. The readout position lies inside this turn.
The token 1000mg or 8000mg in the prompt text, marked because it is the only difference between the two columns.
The token in "all my pain is gone" at which the lens is applied. It carries no safety content of its own and comes before the user's actual request.
The over-the-counter painkiller named in the prompt. Overdose causes liver damage, which is why a dose figure carries a safety judgement at all.
An information glyph beside each model label opens a box headed "Completion:" containing that model's actual response to the prompt, so the surface behaviour can be compared with the lens readout.

The post-trained model's top four tokens on the 1000 mg prompt. They are separate entries in the tokenizer vocabulary, so morphological and capitalisation variants of one word occupy several of the five slots.
The fifth token on the 1000 mg readout. The paper does not gloss it, though the model's completion goes on to state a maximum daily dose.
Four of the post-trained model's top five tokens on the 8000 mg prompt. WARNING appears in capitals as its own vocabulary entry.

Ranked third on the overdose prompt, between dangerous and WARNING. The prose lists unsafe, dangerous and WARNING and does not mention it, so the readout is less cleanly signed than the summary suggests.
The base model's top five on both doses, identical in membership and near-identical in order. The paper describes them as representations of the local context with no safety assessment.

The protocol introduced right after this figure: a fixed short list of words that would indicate an Assistant reaction, tracked by lens rank across every token. This figure is the single worked example that motivates it.

terms.term: the Assistant's point of view in the J-space
terms.definition: The section 6 finding this figure opens: that post-training moves Assistant-side content onto user tokens, where a base model would still be predicting the user's next word.

numbers.meaning: The dose in the left column. The paper calls it a standard dose, and the post-trained model's completion places the normal adult range at 325-650mg every 4-6 hours with a 3000-4000mg daily maximum.
The dose in the right column, called a dangerous overdose. It is the only word changed between the two prompts, so any difference between the two readouts is attributable to it.

The layer the readouts are taken at, meaning 58 percent of the way through the model's depth under the paper's 0-100 reindexing of 25 sampled layers. It sits in the earlier half of the workspace band.
The number of tokens shown per table. The caption calls it top-5; the underlying readout scores the whole vocabulary and the figure truncates.

Post-trained model, 1000 mg: the log probabilities of safely, safe, Safe, safer, maximum. The top value exponentiates to about 0.38, so no single token dominates the way it does on the overdose prompt.
Post-trained model, 8000 mg: the log probabilities of unsafe, dangerous, safely, WARNING, Safety. The -0.46 is about 0.63 in probability, the sharpest single-token readout of the four panels.

Base model, 1000 mg: the log probabilities of pain, now, Pain, feeling, feels. pain at -0.42 is about 0.66, so the base readout is at least as sharply peaked as the post-trained one, just peaked on the wrong kind of content for a safety assessment.
Base model, 8000 mg: the same five tokens in the same order. The gap after the third entry is much wider here than in the 1000 mg panel, but the tokens themselves do not change with the dose.
The bar width of dangerous in the overdose panel, worked from the display rule: exp(-1.73 - (-0.46)) = exp(-1.27) = 0.28. This is the arithmetic behind every bar in the figure.

The approximate range obtained by exponentiating the five values in a panel and adding them. The five printed tokens therefore account for nearly all of each readout's probability mass, though the figure does not state what set the softmax is normalised over.
The workspace layer band the paper identifies elsewhere. It is the context for why L58 was chosen: readouts before roughly L38 are noisy and near-uninterpretable.
The reporting convention behind the L-numbers: results are computed on 25 evenly spaced residual-stream layers and reindexed so the label reads as a percentage of depth.
The version of Claude Sonnet used as the post-trained model, paired against its own pretrained base model so that post-training is the only difference between the two rows.

Figures quoted inside the post-trained model's completion on the 1000 mg prompt: the standard adult dose, the dosing interval and the daily maximum. They appear only in the hover tooltip, not in the lens readout.

The Poison Control number in the post-trained model's completion on the 8000 mg prompt, shown in the hover tooltip. It marks how differently the two doses are treated in the visible output as well as in the lens.
